clue.text: Paddy cried, life in turmoil

definitions.note: a paddy is a flooded field for growing rice

indicators.note: something in turmoil is thrown into disorder, so the letters of the two words are scrambled

explanation.surface: An Irishman named Paddy weeps because his life has fallen apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like an Irishman's name, but it is the definition. 'in turmoil' rearranges CRIED and LIFE together.
explanation.definitionFit: A paddy is a flooded plot where rice is grown, the same thing as a rice field.

clue.text: Port is without additives, from what we hear

indicators.note: this phrase tells us the words before it are said out loud and the entry only matches their sound

parts.note: is gives IS; mere in its old sense means pure, unmixed, with nothing added

explanation.surface: Someone claims a fortified wine is pure, with nothing added, according to rumour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink of the surface, but it is a seaport. IS MERE spoken out loud gives the name of the Turkish city.
explanation.definitionFit: Izmir is a large seaport on Turkey's Aegean coast, formerly called Smyrna.

clue.text: Ordinary fellow Welshman who's name-dropped older citizen?

indicators.note: name-dropped here literally means the letter standing for name has been dropped out of the word before it

parts.note: Jones is the stereotypical Welsh surname, standing for a Welshman
OAP is old-age pensioner, a British term for a retired older person

explanation.surface: A typical bloke from Wales who boasts about knowing famous people is an elderly man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'name-dropped' looks like boasting about famous friends; here it takes the N out of JONES, giving JOES. OAP, old-age pensioner, is British for a retired person.
explanation.definitionFit: Joe Soap is British slang for an average, unremarkable man, like Joe Bloggs or the man in the street.

clue.text: Less uncaring re energy-saving?

indicators.note: less here asks for the phrase minus its outer parts, leaving a run of letters from within those words

explanation.surface: A question about someone becoming more concerned about conserving power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Less' trims away the start of 'uncaring' and the end of 'energy-saving', leaving the run G RE ENER. The whole clue doubles as the definition: a more eco-minded person is less uncaring about saving energy.
explanation.definitionFit: Green means environmentally conscious, so someone more so cares more about conserving energy.

clue.text: Heavy stone could mark it

definitions.meaning: serious, weighty and solemn in manner or importance
a headstone is placed to mark a burial place

explanation.surface: A weighty rock might be placed to mark a spot.
explanation.definitionFit: Grave means serious or weighty, and it is also a burial plot that a headstone marks.

clue.text: To go through concrete, picks up drill

indicators.note: one word going through another sits inside it, so the second piece is placed within the first

parts.note: concrete as an adjective means real, actual
to pick up a sound is to hear it

explanation.surface: Someone takes up a power tool to bore through a slab of concrete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concrete' and 'drill' look like building work; concrete is the adjective meaning real, and drill is practice.
explanation.definitionFit: A drill is a practice run of a routine, just as a rehearsal is a trial performance.

clue.text: Some noise, lovely to the ear

indicators.note: this phrase means the word before it is judged by how it is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: a belle is a lovely woman, a beauty

explanation.surface: A pleasant sound that is easy on the ear.
explanation.walkthrough: BELLE, a beautiful woman, said out loud gives the unit.
explanation.definitionFit: The bel is a unit measuring sound intensity, ten decibels, so it is a measure of some noise.

clue.text: Allowed a dart, maybe, to cross top of board

parts.note: a, as in 'ten pounds a head', means per

indicators.note: the missile crosses the letter in the sense of going over and around it, so the letter sits within

parts.note: a dart is one example of a missile, a thrown weapon

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A player was permitted to throw a dart across the top of a dartboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' does real work: it means per, as in 'twice a day'. 'top of' gives B, which goes inside MISSILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Permissible means allowed or permitted by the rules.

clue.text: Helicopter intercepted by craft got, finally, hit

indicators.note: intercepted means cut into, so the later pieces break into the first word

parts.note: chopper is a slang word for a helicopter
craft means art, skill

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word it follows

explanation.surface: A helicopter was stopped by an aircraft and was finally shot down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' picks T from 'got'. 'hit' looks like shooting down; it is a successful record.
explanation.definitionFit: A hit record is one that reaches number one in the charts.

clue.text: Local news after one

indicators.note: after puts the news pieces second, behind the numeral for one

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I
read as the plural of new, two copies of N, the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood report coming after the first item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' looks like an adjective describing the news; it is the British word for one's neighbourhood pub. 'news' is read as two Ns, N being the abbreviation for new.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain 'the local' is the nearby pub people regularly drink at, and an inn is a pub.

clue.text: Police turned back girl on charity hike

indicators.note: turned back says the word before it is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: the law is a slang term for the police
Kath is a girl's name, short for Katherine
taken as written

explanation.surface: Officers sent a young woman home during a sponsored walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned back' reverses LAW to give WAL; 'girl' gives KATH, a common short form of Katherine.
explanation.definitionFit: A walkathon is a long-distance sponsored walk held to raise money for a good cause.

clue.text: Japanese writing three consecutive letters in return enclosing article

indicators.note: enclosing means the outer letters wrap around the article
in return means the run of letters is read backwards

parts.note: I, J and K follow one another in the alphabet
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A letter in Japanese that comes back with something attached.
explanation.walkthrough: 'three consecutive letters' could be any run of the alphabet; only the run that turns to KJI under 'in return' can hold the article with 'enclosing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Kanji are the Chinese-derived characters used in written Japanese.

clue.text: One used to fasten food on can

indicators.note: in an across clue one word on another is placed after it

parts.note: a can of food is a tin
tack is an old word for food, as in hardtack

explanation.surface: Someone sticks a food label on a can.
explanation.walkthrough: 'food' as TACK is old slang, as in ship's hardtack.
explanation.definitionFit: A tintack is a small tin-coated nail used to fasten things down, such as carpet.

clue.text: Did out old school's outside quarters

parts.note: ex means former, old

indicators.note: the school is outside, so it goes around the pair of compass points

parts.note: a pod is a school of whales or dolphins
S and E are two quarters, or compass points

explanation.surface: Someone excluded the old school because it lay beyond the district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'school' is not a place of learning but a group of whales, and 'quarters' means compass points. 'Did out' means outed or revealed.
explanation.definitionFit: To expose someone is to out them, revealing what they have kept secret.

clue.text: Material such as lead removed from pencil

indicators.note: lead here means the leading letter, which is taken away from the word that follows

parts.note: a crayon is a coloured pencil

explanation.surface: Graphite such as pencil lead has been taken out of a drawing tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead' looks like the graphite in a pencil; here it means the leading letter, C, of CRAYON.
explanation.definitionFit: Rayon is a synthetic fabric made from cellulose, so it is a material.

clue.text: Plays about revolutionary movement: black youths in fifties

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word surrounds the rest

parts.note: to play with something is to toy with it
an eddy is a swirling, circling movement of water
B is the abbreviation for black, as in pencil grades

explanation.surface: Dramas about a political uprising and a black youth movement in the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary movement' looks political; it is a whirling eddy. Teddy boys were 1950s British youths in Edwardian-style suits.
explanation.definitionFit: Teddy boys were a 1950s British youth subculture known for drainpipe trousers and long jackets.

clue.text: Shake-up of rule briefly blocked by judge

indicators.note: blocked by means the word is obstructed by having another piece placed in its middle
briefly means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to reign is to rule

explanation.surface: A judge stopped a reorganisation of the rules.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts REIGN to REIG, and 'blocked by' puts J inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rejig is a rearrangement or reorganisation, a shake-up.

clue.text: Signal to start dancing that's needed during break

parts.note: a cue is a signal for an actor or performer to begin
a ball is a formal dancing party

explanation.surface: A signal for the dancing to begin during an interval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' looks like an interval; it is the opening shot or scoring run in snooker or pool.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker and pool the white ball is struck to make a break, so the game cannot proceed without it.

clue.text: Lifted lid on philanderer, finding alternative to bed?

indicators.note: in a down entry lifted means raised up, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: a lid is a top
re means on or about
a wolf is a man who pursues women

explanation.surface: Someone raised a lid on a womaniser and found an option other than the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' reverses the whole run TOP RE WOLF. 'bed' looks like the bedroom of the surface; it is a flower bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A pot is an alternative to a garden bed for growing flowers.

clue.text: One with seat in room there disturbed insect

indicators.note: in places the member of parliament inside the rearranged letters
disturbed means stirred up, so the letters of the two words are mixed

parts.note: an MP is a member of parliament, someone with a seat in the House

explanation.surface: Someone sitting in a room was disturbed by a bug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disturbed' scrambles the letters of the two words, and 'in' sets the parliamentary member among them; 'seat' means a place in the House of Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: The emperor moth is a large European moth with eyespots on its wings, and a moth is an insect.

clue.text: Appreciated speed — perhaps missing runs

indicators.note: missing means the letter is left out of the word

parts.note: speed is slang for amphetamine, a drug
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Fast pace was valued, though perhaps there were no runs scored.
explanation.walkthrough: 'speed' is an example of a drug, signalled by 'perhaps'. Dropping R leaves the slang sense of liked.
explanation.definitionFit: Dug is dated slang for liked or appreciated, as in 'I dug that record'.

clue.text: Girl not available after losing it?

indicators.note: after means the piece named first comes later in the entry

parts.note: losing it means losing one's temper, which is ire, anger

explanation.surface: A young woman was unavailable after she lost her temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing it' means losing one's temper, giving IRE, anger.
explanation.definitionFit: Irena is a girl's name, a form of Irene.

clue.text: Skirts central section of troubled vessel

parts.note: minis are short skirts

indicators.note: the central section means the middle two letters of the word

explanation.surface: Short skirts at the heart of a distressed ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'central section of' takes UB from the middle of 'troubled'.
explanation.definitionFit: A mini-sub is a small submarine, and a submarine is a vessel.

clue.text: Country retreat houses a senior minister

parts.note: rural means of the country

indicators.note: houses means holds inside, so the article goes within the den

parts.note: a den is a private retreat

explanation.surface: A rural hideaway is home to an important clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minister' is not a politician but a clergyman. A rural dean leads the clergy in a district.
explanation.definitionFit: A rural dean is a senior Anglican priest supervising a group of parishes.

clue.text: Turn from odd pair behind foot of pavilion

indicators.note: odd means strange, so these letters are put in an unusual order
in a down clue the foot of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A turn made by a strange couple behind the cricket pavilion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foot of' gives N, the last letter of 'pavilion', which is shuffled with PAIR BEHIND.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairpin bend is a very sharp U-shaped turn in a road.

clue.text: Champion, note, stopping fighting where there's been no progress?

parts.note: to champion a cause is to back it

indicators.note: stopping means plugging, so the note sits inside the word for fighting

parts.note: war is fighting
te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A champion's music stops the fighting, though nothing has moved forward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Champion' is a verb here, giving BACK.
explanation.definitionFit: A backwater is a stagnant place untouched by progress or new ideas.

clue.text: Money one's out to get?

parts.note: reads as money someone is chasing, but 'out' means on strike, so it is the allowance paid to workers who have walked out

explanation.definitionFit: Strike pay is the money a trade union pays members while they are on strike.

clue.text: Play with ten collapsing in heaps

indicators.note: collapsing means falling apart, so these letters are reassembled in a new order

explanation.surface: A play performed with ten actors falls apart in heaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapsing' rearranges PLAY and TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplenty means in abundance, which is what in heaps means.

clue.text: An old dramatist, I love touring singles clubs

indicators.note: touring means going around, so the first pair of letters goes around the rest

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
singles are ones
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: Someone says they love going around nightclubs for single people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' puts I and O around ONES and C.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Ionesco, who died in 1994, was a Romanian-French playwright of the Theatre of the Absurd.

clue.text: Catch up with answer another time

indicators.note: with here means the reply's letter is set alongside, ahead of the verb's letters

parts.note: to gain on someone is to catch up with them

explanation.surface: A request to meet up again to deliver a reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch up' gives GAIN, as in gaining on a rival.
explanation.definitionFit: Again means once more, on another occasion.

clue.text: Go off working hard for Asian banker

indicators.note: off means taken away, so the letters for an attempt are removed

parts.note: industry is hard work, diligence
a go is a try, an attempt

explanation.surface: Someone stops toiling at a job for an Asian financier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banker' is not a financier but something with banks, a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indus is a great river of Pakistan and northern India, and a river has banks.

clue.text: Young Tom's first half tackle

indicators.note: first half takes the opening three of the six letters

parts.note: a tom is a male cat, and a young cat is a kitten

explanation.surface: A boy called Tom's first half of football equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tom' looks like a boy; it is a tom cat, whose young is a KITTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: Tackle means equipment or gear, as does kit.
